title: Implementation & Simulation
why: The largest tag on Codeforces. These problems have no clever idea — they test whether you can translate a fussy statement into correct code without a single off-by-one. Speed here directly buys you time for the hard problems later in a contest.
traps: Reading the statement diagonally. Implementation problems punish skimming more than any other category.
1-indexed input vs 0-indexed arrays. Pick one convention and convert at read time, not scattered through the code.
Not handling n = 1 or an empty result. Almost every implementation failure is a boundary case.
Writing everything in main(). Split into small functions so you can test pieces.

template.py:
# Read the statement TWICE, outline as comments, then fill in.

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

# 1. ...
# 2. ...
# 3. ...

checkpoint: You can solve a Div2 A in under 10 minutes with no failed submissions, five contests in a row.

title: Sorting with Custom Keys
why: An enormous number of problems become trivial once the data is in the right order. The real skill is spotting *which* order: sort by deadline, by ratio, by end time, by the difference between two fields.
traps: Sorting pairs and forgetting that the default compares the second element too when firsts tie — sometimes that's what you want, often it isn't.
Losing original indices. If you need them, sort an array of (value, index) pairs.
Writing a comparator that isn't a strict weak ordering (returning true for equal elements). In C++ this is undefined behaviour and can crash.
Sorting when you only need the k largest — `nth_element` / `heapq.nlargest` is O(n).

template.py:
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
idx = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: a[i])          # indices in sorted order

pairs = sorted(zip(a, range(n)))                    # by value, then index
pairs.sort(key=lambda p: (-p[0], p[1]))             # value desc, index asc

import heapq
top_k = heapq.nlargest(k, a)                        # O(n log k)

pyNote: `sorted(range(n), key=...)` is the clean Python way to sort indices without building pair tuples. Tuple keys `(-x, y)` handle mixed asc/desc without a comparator.
checkpoint: Given a greedy problem, you can identify and justify the correct sort order before writing any code.

title: String Fundamentals
why: Strings are just arrays of characters, but the character-arithmetic idioms (`c - 'a'`), frequency counting over the 26 letters, and the cost of concatenation are worth making automatic.
traps: In C++, `s + t` inside a loop is O(n^2). Use `+=`, which is amortised O(1).
Python strings are immutable — building with `s += c` in a loop is O(n^2). Append to a list and `''.join()` at the end.
`s[i] - '0'` for digits vs `s[i] - 'a'` for letters — mixing these up silently produces garbage indices.
Comparing a `char` to a string literal: `s[i] == "a"` doesn't compile in C++; you need `'a'`.

template.py:
s = input().strip()
n = len(s)

from collections import Counter
cnt = Counter(s)                        # or: [0]*26 with ord(c) - ord('a')

out = ''.join(c for c in s if c != 'x') # NOT out += c in a loop

is_pal = s == s[::-1]
sub = s[i:i+length]

pyNote: Python slicing makes reversal and substring extraction trivial, but each slice copies — a loop of O(n) slices is O(n^2). Use indices when you only need to compare.
checkpoint: You can count character frequencies and test palindromes without thinking, in both languages.

title: Elementary Math
why: Integer overflow, parity arguments, and gcd show up constantly. Many Div2 A/B problems are pure observation: notice the answer depends only on n mod 2, and you're done in three lines.
traps: **Overflow.** In C++, `int * int` overflows at ~2*10^9 even when assigned to a `long long`. Cast one operand: `(ll)a * b`.
C++ `%` on negative numbers returns a negative result; Python's `%` always returns non-negative. This difference bites when porting.
Integer division truncates toward zero in C++ but floors in Python. `-7/2` is -3 in C++ and -4 in Python.
Using floating point for exact comparisons. `sqrt(n)` can be off by one — verify with integer multiplication.

template.py:
from math import gcd, isqrt

g = gcd(a, b)
l = a // g * b

# Python ints are arbitrary precision - overflow does not exist
prod = a * b

up = -(-a // b)          # ceiling division, works for negatives too
r = isqrt(n)             # exact integer sqrt, no float error ever

pyNote: This is where Python genuinely wins: arbitrary-precision integers mean no overflow bugs ever, and `math.isqrt` is exact. Problems involving huge factorials or 10^18 products are far easier in Python.
checkpoint: You have been bitten by C++ overflow once, found it, and now cast reflexively.

title: Complete Search
why: When constraints are small, the correct move is to try everything. Recognising that n <= 20 means 'enumerate all 2^n subsets' or n <= 100 means 'try all pairs' is a decision you make from the constraints, not from cleverness.
traps: Not checking whether brute force actually fits. Compute the count first: C(100,3) is 161700 — fine. C(100,5) is 75 million — not fine.
Nested loops that redo work. Precompute anything loop-invariant outside the inner loop.
Forgetting that a brute force over *answers* is often smaller than over inputs — try each possible answer and verify it.
pyNote: `itertools` makes brute force shorter in Python than C++ — `combinations`, `permutations` and `product` cover nearly every enumeration you need, and they run at C speed.
checkpoint: You can compute the exact operation count of a brute force and decide go/no-go in under 30 seconds.

title: Greedy Basics
why: Greedy means: repeatedly take the locally best option and never reconsider. It's the most common Div2 A/B technique and also the most commonly *wrong* one — the discipline is proving (or at least stress-testing) that local optimality implies global optimality.
traps: Assuming greedy works because it passes the samples. Samples are small and kind. Stress test against a brute force.
Not identifying what to be greedy *on*. Sort by the right key and the greedy is obvious; sort by the wrong one and it's simply incorrect.
Problems where greedy fails and DP is needed — the classic tell is that an early choice constrains later ones in a non-obvious way (e.g. 0/1 knapsack).
Forgetting ties. When two options look equally good, the tiebreak sometimes matters.

template.py:
# maximum non-overlapping intervals -> sort by END
iv.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])
cnt, last_end = 0, float('-inf')
for s, e in iv:
    if s >= last_end:
        cnt += 1
        last_end = e

# pair largest with smallest
a.sort()
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo < hi:
    total += a[lo] + a[hi]
    lo += 1
    hi -= 1

checkpoint: You can state, in one sentence, why your greedy is correct — an exchange argument, not 'it passed'.

title: Frequency Counting & Hashing
why: 'How many times does X appear' and 'have I seen X before' underlie a huge fraction of easy problems. A hash map turns an O(n^2) scan into O(n).
traps: In C++, `mp[key]` *inserts* a default-constructed value if the key is absent. Use `mp.count(key)` or `mp.find(key)` to test membership without inserting.
`unordered_map<int,int>` on Codeforces is hackable — an adversary can craft keys that all collide, making it O(n^2). Add a random hash or use `map` in hacked-prone problems.
Iterating an `unordered_map` gives unspecified order; if the answer depends on order, you'll get non-deterministic wrong answers.
Counting pairs: when you scan and ask 'how many previous elements satisfy X', add to the map *after* querying, not before.

template.py:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

cnt = Counter(a)
if x in cnt: pass                 # never inserts

seen = defaultdict(int)
pairs = 0
for x in a:
    pairs += seen[k - x]          # query BEFORE inserting
    seen[x] += 1

# most common elements
for val, c in cnt.most_common(3):
    print(val, c)

pyNote: `Counter` does in one line what takes four in C++, and `most_common()` is free. Python dicts are not hackable on Codeforces the way C++ `unordered_map` is, since the hash is randomised per run.
checkpoint: You can count pairs summing to k in a single pass, and explain why querying before inserting matters.

title: 2D Grids
why: Grid problems are everywhere, and they all share the same skeleton: bounds checking and a direction array. Getting this idiom right once removes a whole class of off-by-one and out-of-bounds bugs.
traps: Mixing up (row, col) and (x, y). Pick row-major and stay there.
Forgetting bounds checks before indexing — in C++ this is silent memory corruption, not a crash.
In Python, `grid = [[0]*m]*n` creates n references to the *same* row. Use a comprehension.
Diagonal moves: 4 directions vs 8. Read the statement carefully.

template.py:
n, m = map(int, input().split())
g = [input().strip() for _ in range(n)]

grid = [[0]*m for _ in range(n)]      # NOT [[0]*m]*n

DIRS = ((-1,0), (1,0), (0,-1), (0,1))

for dr, dc in DIRS:
    nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
    if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < m:
        ...  # Python chained comparison makes bounds checks clean

pyNote: `0 <= nr < n` chained comparison is both faster and clearer than two separate checks. Watch the `[[0]*m]*n` aliasing trap — it is the single most common Python grid bug.
checkpoint: You can write a bounds-checked 4-direction grid traversal from memory in under a minute.
